opus-5.5.text:
I think the cleanest way to see it is as a hierarchy, but a leaky one.

At the top you have task-level decisions: which object to pick up, in what order, whether to push something aside first, when to regrasp. That level reasons about goals and discrete choices, and it's increasingly where large models are useful, because they bring common sense about the world. At the bottom you have low-level control: joint torques, impedance, reacting to contact at hundreds or thousands of hertz. That level is about physics, stability, and timing.

Classically, people drew a hard line between the two. The planner outputs a sequence of waypoints or primitives, and the controller tracks them. That works well in structured settings like factories, where the world matches the plan. But in messy, contact-rich manipulation, the line breaks down. Whether a grasp is a good *decision* depends on whether the controller can actually *execute* it. Can the fingers get around the object, will it slip, will the cloth bunch up? So the high level can't be ignorant of low-level capability, and the low level often has to make small decisions of its own, like adjusting when it feels unexpected resistance.

So my view is that the interface between them is the real research question. You want the high level to speak in terms that are abstract enough to generalize, but grounded enough that they're actually achievable. And you want feedback flowing upward: when the low level fails or struggles, that should inform the next decision rather than just being an error.

Learning-based approaches, where you train policies end to end or with learned intermediate representations, are blurring the boundary further. I don't think the hierarchy disappears, because there are real differences in timescale and in what each level needs to know. But I think the best systems will treat it less as a chain of command and more as a conversation between the two levels.

r001.rationale: The response mentions waypoints or primitives as planner outputs and joint torques as low-level control, but does not identify joint-position commands as the interface.

r002.rationale: It says low-level failures or struggles should inform the next decision, but does not explain that the task-level controller uses the scene observed after an action to choose its next action.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most useful way to see it is that they're not two separate layers that talk to each other through a thin interface. They're one problem that we've historically chopped in two because our tools couldn't handle it whole.

The classic picture is a planner sitting on top, saying "grasp the cup, move it to the shelf," and a controller underneath, taking that command and tracking a trajectory at a thousand hertz. It's clean, and for a long time it was the only thing that worked. But the seam between them is where most of the failures actually live. The planner assumes the world is roughly what it thought it was. The controller assumes the plan is roughly feasible. When the cup is slippery, or the shelf is two centimeters off, neither layer owns the mistake. The planner doesn't feel it, and the controller doesn't understand it.

So what I care about is how much information flows back up. A good controller is a sensor for the task level. Contact forces, tracking error, how hard the arm is working to hold a pose, those are all telling you something about whether the task-level belief about the world was right. If the task layer never hears that, you get a robot that executes beautifully and fails confidently.

The other direction matters just as much. Task-level intent should change what "good control" means. Pouring water and inserting a connector are both "move the end effector," but one wants smoothness and the other wants compliance in a specific direction. If the controller only ever sees a target pose, it can't make that choice. Something higher has to hand down not just where to go, but what to care about along the way.

Where it gets interesting now is that learned policies are starting to blur the line on purpose. A policy that outputs actions at fifty or a hundred hertz, directly from images and proprioception, is doing a bit of both at once. It's making a small task decision and a small control decision in the same step. People sometimes read that as "control is dead, just learn end to end." I don't read it that way. I think it's more that the boundary is becoming a design choice rather than a given. You still want something fast and stable at the bottom that keeps the hardware safe when the policy is wrong, because it will be wrong. But you can let the boundary move depending on the task and how much data you have.

If I had to put it in one sentence: task-level decisions tell you what to pay attention to, low-level control tells you what's actually happening, and the whole game is making sure those two keep talking fast enough to matter.

r001.rationale: The response discusses target poses and actions as information passed between levels, but never identifies joint-position commands as their interface.

r002.rationale: It describes feedback reaching the task level, but does not clearly state that the task-level controller uses the scene observed after an action to choose its next action.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as two parts of a feedback loop. The task level decides what the arm should accomplish—pick up this object, move it somewhere, release it—and the low-level controller turns that intention into motion while responding to what’s actually happening.

But the task planner can’t just issue commands and assume they succeed. If the gripper slips, or the arm encounters unexpected resistance, that information needs to go back up so the system can adjust its plan. Likewise, the planner needs to respect what the controller can physically achieve.

So the key is the interface between them: goals and constraints going down, and feedback about progress, uncertainty, and failure coming back up. You want a useful separation of responsibilities, but continuous communication.

r002.rationale: It says feedback about progress, uncertainty, and failure should go back to the planner, but does not explain that the task-level controller uses the scene observed after an action to choose its next action.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as two parts of a feedback loop. The task level decides what the arm should accomplish—pick up a cup, for example—and breaks that goal into steps. The low-level controller turns those steps into motion while responding to what the robot senses.

But the relationship has to work in both directions. If the controller detects unexpected contact or can’t reach a pose safely, that information should change the plan. Maybe the arm needs a different grasp, or maybe it needs to stop and observe again.

So the key is the interface: the task level should express goals and constraints, and the controller should report whether those goals are feasible and how execution is going. A good plan has to respect the physical capabilities of the arm.

r001.rationale: The response describes an interface of goals, constraints, and execution feedback, but does not identify joint-position commands.

r002.rationale: It says sensing unexpected contact or unsafe reach should change the plan, such as choosing a different grasp or stopping to observe again, communicating that observations during execution inform what happens next.
